---

Papers are read against six fields, in the order below, so entries stay comparable. The
papers the pipeline itself is built on are cited on the [Resources](resources.qmd) page.

## How each paper is read

**1. Year published**
: Establishes what was technically possible at the time. A 2010 microarray study and a 2025
deep-proteomics study are not making the same kind of claim.

**2. Model(s) used**
: Which species, whether the comparison is within or across species, and whether the
cross-species claim rests on the same tissue.

**3. Brain region**
: Recorded whenever stated. **Cerebrovascular endothelium differs between brain regions**,
and between arterial, capillary and venous segments of the same vessel tree, so a gene
"BBB-enriched" in one region or segment may not be in another. Where a paper does not state
the region — or where regions are not matched between species — that is recorded too.

**4. What is measured**
: DNA, RNA, or protein. Sequence conservation and expression answer different questions, and
a paper measuring RNA cannot on its own support a claim about conservation.

**5. How it is measured**
: Microarray, bulk RNA-seq, single-cell/nucleus RNA-seq, proteomics, genomic sequencing. For
RNA-seq, **bulk or single-cell**, and whether cells were sorted. Bulk brain tissue drowns
endothelial signal in neurons; isolated microvessels or sorted endothelium do not.

**6. Statistical and modelling techniques**
: What was done to compare across species — orthologue assignment, differential tests and
thresholds, alignment, selection estimates, phylogenetic versus pairwise, multiple-testing
correction.

## Papers

### Kumabe et al. 2025 {#kumabe2025}

> Kumabe H, Masuda T, Ito S, Furihata T, Toda A, Mogi M, Araki N, Ohtsuki S (2025).
> Proteome profile differences among human, monkey, and mouse brain microvessels and cultured
> brain microvascular endothelial cells. *Fluids and Barriers of the CNS* 22:53.
> <https://doi.org/10.1186/s12987-025-00650-z>. Open Access.

| Field | |
|---|---|
| **Year** | 2025 (published online 30 May 2025) |
| **Models** | Human, cynomolgus monkey (*Macaca fascicularis*), mouse (C57BL/6N). Plus cultured cells: MBEC4 (immortalised mouse), hCMEC/D3 and HBMEC/ciβ (immortalised human), primary human BMECs, and HUVEC as a peripheral endothelial comparator |
| **Brain region** | **Not matched between species.** Human and monkey: frozen *cerebral cortex*. Mouse: whole *cerebrum*. Sub-region and vessel segment not resolved — microvessels are isolated as a bulk fraction |
| **Measures** | **Protein** (primary). **RNA** secondary — bulk RNA-seq, cultured cells only, not brain tissue |
| **Method** | Brain microvessels (BMVs) isolated from frozen brain. Untargeted **DIA** LC-MS/MS, library-free search in DIA-NN 1.8.1. **QTAP** with isotope-labelled standards for SLC43A3. **Western blot** for enrichment control. Bulk RNA-seq for cultured cells |
| **Cross-species stats** | Mouse→human orthologues via Alliance of Genome Resources. Mean ± SD; two-tailed Student's *t*-test; one-way ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc; Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted *p*. PCA and hierarchical clustering. GO enrichment (DAVID 2011) |

: {tbl-colwidths="[22,78]"}

#### My reading

The paper is about differences in the **BBB proteome** — the full set of proteins in the
blood-brain barrier — and specifically about differences **in vitro against in vivo**, using
proteomic analysis. Most of the work is on **brain microvessels (BMVs)**; cultured brain
microvascular endothelial cells come in towards the end.

There are a lot of results. They look at **claudin-5** specifically, at the **SLC
transporters** and their expression in vivo and in vitro for all three species, and at the
brain microvessel dataset for all three species. Because of the **clustering, monkey and
human BMVs are the ones that correlate** — those two go together, mouse sits apart.

**Background (p2).** They set up from papers that had already looked at human, monkey, rat
and pig, and at species differences in the blood-brain barrier in mouse, human and monkey.
Their approach is protein expression profiling using **QTAP** — quantitative absolute
targeted proteomics — applied to in vivo protein expression in BMVs. They also use
**immortalised cells**. They explain where their cells came from, mainly real brains, and
the isolation of microvessels from frozen brain for all three species.

**Methods.** Protein concentration measured with a **bicinchoninic acid (BCA) protein assay
kit**. Then cell culture — how the cells were grown and what was used. Then cell sample
preparation for proteomic analysis; I read this but not in full depth. Then the crude
membrane fraction for proteome analysis. Then **Western blot analysis** — I did not really
understand what this one does.

Then the quantitative proteomic analysis: trypsin digestion with the PTS method for mouse,
human and cultured cells, analysed by **DIA** and mass spectrometry. The monkey BMV and
mouse BMV samples were analysed on a **Dionex Ultimate** system. Proteins were identified
using the **library-free search** function in DIA-NN.

For the monkey samples they **compared against the human proteome, because there is not
enough monkey data**. They then normalised their quantitative values using the formula on
p4 — that equation is the normalisation of the protein expression values they obtained.

Mouse genes were converted into the corresponding human genes using **Alliance of Genome
Resources** as orthologues — but I noted that the orthologues they have are **not
one-to-one**; there are multiple.

Then the transporters: QTAP for **SLC43A3**. Then RNA sequencing — they quantified mRNA
concentration, though I am not certain exactly what for; I assume for every species.

**Statistics.** Mean and standard deviation. A **two-tailed Student's *t*-test** in Microsoft
Excel. Multiple groups compared using **one-way ANOVA** — I know what ANOVA is, comparing
multiple averages, but not specifically one-way — followed by **Tukey post-hoc tests**.
Because they have multiple *p*-values, these were adjusted with the **Benjamini–Hochberg**
method, which they refer to as the adjusted *p*-value. Separately, **GO enrichment analysis**
using DAVID 2011.

**Results — isolation.** They isolated microvessels from frozen cerebrum and cerebral
cortices, and used Western blotting to evaluate microvessel enrichment in the isolated
fractions. **Claudin-5** was detected in the BMV fractions of all species. **PSD95**, a
neuronal marker, was detected in the brain lysates of all species but **not** in the
microvessel fraction. From that they conclude the microvessels were enriched in the isolated
fractions, and that proteomic analysis could be conducted with similar enrichment across
biological replicates of all species. So they are also showing that **their method is
reproducible**, and this is why it is a strong method.

**Results — proteomic analysis of isolated BMVs.** DIA proteomics. They state that the
monkey proteome database is incomplete — important proteins could not be found. What they
did find is that the number of identified proteins in the BMV fractions and brain lysates was
**not significantly different** between data analysed with the monkey and the human reference
proteome databases, which is a good case for them given the incomplete monkey data. The
quantified values also significantly correlate between the monkey and human reference
databases, and they argue this from the *p*-value.

**Results — cultured BMECs.** Proteomic and RNA-seq analysis. In all samples the **number of
identified genes was greater than the number of proteins**. This section is specifically
their argumentation that the method and quantification are reproducible and strong.

**Results — comparing the three species.** They identify around **12,000 orthologous
proteins**, and almost **7,000 proteins identified in all three species**, which is a huge
chunk. They discuss possible contamination of the fractions, but according to the *p*-value
this should not have had a large impact on the data. Then **clustering and PCA** for the
proteome profile of the BMV fractions in all three species.

**Results — transport-related proteins.** Species differences in transport-related protein
expression in BMVs, using QTAP to assess the reproducibility of the multi-species proteome
data — so again, checking that the method is sound.

Then several pages of graphs. I marked a lot here, but in general **the paragraphs after p10
all go back to the method being reproducible**, plus the point that some transport-related
proteins are more expressed in the enriched BMV fractions than in brain lysates, with
*p*-values for some of those. **This section was incredibly hard to read.**

**Results — in vivo against in vitro.** Comparing the proteome profile between BMV fractions
and cultured BMECs, again using PCA and clustering. **Primary cultured human BMECs had the
closest profile to the human BMV fraction.**

**Results — claudins (p11).** Differences between in vitro and in vivo: in vivo, expression
levels were higher in the brain microvessel fractions. And per subtype of the claudin family
there were different expression levels between BMVs, cultured BMECs and the cell lines.

**Discussion.** They argue that their deep proteomic profile of BMV fractions from isolated
human, monkey and mouse brain, together with the profile of cultured BBB model cells,
provides a good starting point for future research to build on. They discuss which proteins
were identified and how reproducible the data are.

**Notes past p13** *(printer cut off, so these are from reading rather than annotation)*:

- Blood removal is **not statistically significant** for the species differences of
  BMV-enriched proteins.
- There is **high transport-related protein correlation between human and monkey**.
- The transporters the study focused on: **SLC43A3**, **SLC22A6** and **SLCO**, in all three
  species and their respective BMV fractions.
- The **in vivo / in vitro comparison revealed differences in the expression levels of
  transporters involved in the transport of amino acids and DHA** — and the same goes for the
  claudin family.

#### What I take from it

Reading it through, **a large part of this paper is the authors arguing that their method is
reproducible and robust**, rather than reporting biology. The enrichment check, the monkey-
versus-human database comparison, the gene-count-versus-protein-count comparison, the QTAP
re-measurement — each of these sections exists to defend the data, and they recur after
almost every result. The biological findings sit inside that scaffolding rather than driving
the paper.

That is not a criticism. For a multi-species proteomics dataset intended as a reference
resource, the method validation *is* the contribution — and it is the part of this paper that
is most worth borrowing.

#### Open questions from this read

- What does a Western blot actually do, and why is it the right check here? *(answered in the
  [glossary](#methods-glossary) below)*
- What is "one-way" ANOVA, as opposed to other kinds? *(glossary)*
- What is a Tukey post-hoc test for? *(glossary)*
- What does "immortalised" mean for a cell line, and what does it cost you? *(glossary)*
- The cell sample preparation and crude membrane sections — read, but not in depth. Worth
  returning to if the method is ever borrowed.
- The RNA sequencing: what exactly was it for, and on which samples? *(cultured cells only,
  not brain tissue — confirmed against the paper)*
- The transport-related results after p10 were hard to read. Worth a second pass.

#### How it relates to this project

1. **Independent, non-sequence support for the macaque result.** This project's clearest
   surviving finding is that macaque coding sequence sits closer to human than mouse does.
   Kumabe reaches the same ordering from a completely different measurement — protein
   expression in isolated microvessels. Two modalities agreeing is worth more than either
   alone. They remain different claims: conservation of *sequence* versus similarity of
   *expression*.

2. **It is a primate BBB dataset, which this project does not have.** The
   [audit](audit.qmd) records that there is no macaque expression evidence at all — every
   gene earned its place from a mouse study, and the paper logged as the macaque dataset
   contained no macaque samples. Kumabe supplies that missing layer, at protein level.

   **Caveat before using it:** this is **cynomolgus** macaque (*Macaca fascicularis*). This
   project's macaque genome is **rhesus** (*Macaca mulatta*, Mmul_10). Different species —
   close, but not interchangeable without saying so.

3. **The brain-region field earned its place immediately.** Human and monkey samples are
   cerebral cortex; mouse is whole cerebrum. Any mouse-versus-primate difference here is
   partly confounded with region. The authors are open about their other confounders too —
   longer post-mortem interval in the human samples, perfusion in mice only — and they test
   the blood-contamination one directly.

4. **The same orthologue problem, named out loud.** The observation about orthologues not
   being one-to-one is exactly this project's problem: one-to-many pairs at 25.8% identity
   entering the BBB set in `step3b`, and `step5d` then applying different orthologue rules to
   the BBB and control sets.

5. **A better human validation set than the one currently used.** `step4b` validates the gene
   list against a single arterial marker sheet. Kumabe's BMV-enriched protein lists are a
   defined, thresholded, protein-level alternative — and they exist for a primate as well as
   for human.

#### Reference detail from the paper

Numbers to cite from, checked against the text.

- **Depth:** 7,149–8,274 proteins per BMV fraction; 6,657–7,534 in whole-brain lysate.
- **Orthologues:** 12,272 orthologous proteins total; **6,845 identified in all three
  species**.
- **BMV-enriched** (log₂ BMV/brain > 2.5, adjusted *p* < 0.05): 1,636 mouse, 1,166 monkey,
  2,155 human; 528 shared across all three.
- **Monkey database validation:** protein intensities from the monkey and human reference
  databases correlate at *r* = 0.888 (*p* < 0.0001); 75.6% of proteins within 1.5-fold.
  Human–monkey genomic difference taken as ~4%.
- **Species differences in transporters:** ABCB1/Abcb1a higher in mouse (human/mouse ratio
  0.344); ABCG2/Abcg2 2.57-fold higher in monkey than human; SLC22A8/Slc22a8 and
  SLC22A6/Slc22a6 detected in mouse only; SLCO1A2 quantified in human where mouse expresses
  Slco1a4 and Slco1c1; **SLC43A3/Slc43a3 is primate-specific** — present in human and monkey
  BMVs, absent in mouse, confirmed by QTAP at 22.4-fold higher in hCMEC/D3 than MBEC4.
- **In vitro against in vivo:** ABCC1 11.3-fold and SLC29A1 1.54-fold higher in hCMEC/D3 than
  in BMVs; SLC7A5 5.79-fold higher in BMVs; **claudin-5 not detected at all in hCMEC/D3**.
  Immortalised lines clustered closer to HUVEC than to primary BMECs. MFSD2A absent from
  cultured cells entirely.
- **Claudins:** total claudin family expression higher in BMVs in vivo; claudin-5 highest in
  BMVs, claudin-11 high in most cell lines, claudin-12 the major subtype in MBEC4.


## Methods glossary

Terms from the papers, explained once.

**Immortalised cells**
: A cell line engineered to divide indefinitely, usually by inserting a gene such as SV40 T
antigen or telomerase. Ordinary primary cells taken from tissue divide a limited number of
times and then stop, which makes them awkward to work with; immortalised lines are
convenient, reproducible and cheap. The cost is that they drift away from the original
tissue — which is precisely what Kumabe measures: hCMEC/D3 and HBMEC/ciβ resemble generic
vein endothelium (HUVEC) more than they resemble real brain microvessels, and hCMEC/D3 has
lost claudin-5 entirely.

**Western blot**
: A method to check whether one specific protein is present, and roughly how much. Proteins
are separated by size in a gel, transferred onto a membrane, and probed with an antibody that
binds only the target. Here it is a quality control, not a result: claudin-5 present in the
microvessel fraction shows the fraction contains endothelium; PSD95 absent shows it is not
contaminated with neurons. β-actin is the loading control — it should be equal in every lane,
confirming equal amounts of protein were loaded.

**DIA — data-independent acquisition**
: A mass-spectrometry strategy. In the older data-*dependent* approach the instrument picks
the most intense peptides to fragment and measure, so weakly abundant proteins are missed and
different runs measure different things. DIA fragments *everything* in successive mass
windows, so the same proteins are measured in every run. That is why this study can compare
across species and samples with confidence, and why it reaches 7,000–8,000 proteins.

**QTAP — quantitative targeted absolute proteomics**
: Instead of relative abundance, this measures the actual molar amount of a chosen protein,
by spiking in a synthetic version of one of its peptides labelled with heavy isotopes. The
known standard and the real peptide behave identically but differ in mass, so the ratio gives
an absolute concentration. Used here to confirm the SLC43A3 result independently of DIA.

**BCA assay (bicinchoninic acid)**
: A colour-change assay for total protein concentration in a sample. Used so that equal
amounts of protein go into each analysis.

**Two-tailed Student's *t*-test**
: Tests whether the means of **two** groups differ. "Two-tailed" means it tests for a
difference in either direction — higher *or* lower — rather than predicting the direction in
advance. Two-tailed is the conservative default.

**One-way ANOVA**
: The extension of the *t*-test to **three or more** groups, with "one-way" meaning the groups
differ along a single factor — here, species. It answers only "are these groups all the
same?", not which pair differs. Running repeated *t*-tests between every pair instead would
inflate the false-positive rate, which is the problem ANOVA exists to avoid.

**Tukey post-hoc test**
: Run *after* a significant ANOVA to find *which* pairs actually differ, while correcting for
the fact that you are making several comparisons at once.

**Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment**
: A multiple-testing correction. Testing thousands of proteins at *p* < 0.05 produces many
false positives by chance alone. BH controls the **false discovery rate** — the expected
proportion of claimed hits that are wrong — and is less severe than Bonferroni, which is why
it suits large screens. The corrected value is the "adjusted *p*-value". This project uses
both, in `step5g`.

**PCA — principal component analysis**
: Compresses thousands of measurements per sample into a few axes that capture most of the
variation, so samples can be plotted and compared. When human and monkey sit near each other
on PC1 and mouse sits apart, that is a statement about overall proteome similarity.

**Hierarchical clustering**
: Repeatedly joins the two most similar samples until everything is in one tree. The
branching order and branch heights show which samples group together and how strongly —
independent confirmation of what the PCA shows.

**GO enrichment analysis**
: Gene Ontology assigns standard functional labels to genes and proteins. Enrichment asks
whether a list contains more of a given label than chance would give — here, showing that
BMV-enriched proteins are disproportionately "transmembrane transporter activity" and
"maintenance of blood-brain barrier". DAVID is the tool that performs this test.

**TPM — transcripts per million**
: A normalised unit of RNA-seq expression, adjusted for both sequencing depth and transcript
length so values can be compared between genes and samples.
